nameStory: Desmodesmus communis doesn't have a widely recognized common name since it's a microscopic green alga that most people never see without magnification. The scientific name 'Desmodesmus' means 'chain-bound' in Greek, referring to how these tiny cells link together in groups of four or eight. The species name 'communis' means 'common' - though ironically, this particular species has only been recorded once in New England!
description: This is a microscopic freshwater green alga - a simple plant-like organism made up of just a few cells stuck together. You'll never see individual Desmodesmus communis with the naked eye, as each cell is smaller than the width of a human hair. Under a microscope, it appears as small groups of 4-8 bright green, oval-shaped cells arranged in neat rows. Unlike the plants we typically think of, this alga has no roots, stems, or leaves - just simple cells that float freely in pond water.

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Cells are organized in flat, rectangular colonies of 4-8 cells arranged in alternating rows - like tiny green bricks stacked in a wall pattern

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are oval to egg-shaped with smooth, curved edges - no spines or projections like some related algae

idTips.label: Size scale
idTips.description: Entire colonies measure 15-30 micrometers across - about 1/3 the width of a human hair, requiring at least 400x magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Color appearance
idTips.description: Bright grass-green color throughout, sometimes with a slightly yellowish tint in older colonies

idTips.label: Cell walls
idTips.description: Outer cells in the colony often have thickened walls that appear slightly darker green under the microscope

habitat: Found floating freely in the water column of freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and is often most abundant in areas with some organic matter or gentle water movement. May be more common in warmer, shallow areas of water bodies during growing season.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures rise above 50°F, often appearing first in shallow, sun-warmed areas of ponds and lakes.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most numerous and easiest to find in water samples. Reproduces rapidly in warm water.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight hours shorten in late autumn.
seasonality.winter: Likely dormant or present in very low numbers under ice cover, surviving as resistant cells until spring warming.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these tiny algae colonies - meaning you've probably unknowingly swallowed millions of them if you've ever accidentally gotten pond water in your mouth while swimming!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's easily confused with other Scenedesmus-family algae that also form small cell colonies. The key is counting cells (Desmodesmus typically has 4-8 while true Scenedesmus often has just 4) and checking for spines - Desmodesmus communis has smooth cells while many relatives have tiny spikes or projections.
contextualKnowledge: This organism represents the often-overlooked microscopic plant life that forms the base of aquatic food webs. What we call 'pond scum' or 'green water' is usually made up of billions of these types of algae, which produce oxygen and feed countless tiny animals.
compareHints: Compared to its Desmodesmus relatives, D. communis has the smoothest cell walls with no spines or teeth-like projections. While D. denticulatus has obvious tooth-like spines and D. protuberans has bumpy protrusions, D. communis maintains clean, oval cell shapes. This makes it one of the more 'plain' looking species in the genus, but also one of the most distinctive once you know what to look for.
